1950.title: Chasing the Alfa Romeos.
1950.story: Ferrari’s first championship season brought Ascari two second places, at Monaco and Monza. The Monza result came in Dorino Serafini’s car, a shared drive, after his own new 4.5-litre Ferrari retired.

1951.title: The first victories.
1951.story: Wins at the Nürburgring and Monza, his first in the championship, took Ascari to the Spanish finale with a title chance. Tyre trouble there left him fourth, and runner-up to Fangio.

1952.title: Six starts, six victories.
1952.story: Ascari missed the Swiss opener to race at the Indianapolis 500, then a championship round, and retired there. He won all six remaining rounds and became Ferrari’s first drivers’ champion.

1953.title: The first to defend it.
1953.story: Five wins, from Buenos Aires to Bremgarten, made Ascari the first driver to retain the world title. At Monza he spun on the final corner while fighting for victory.

1954.title: One more race in red.
1954.story: Contracted to Lancia, whose D50 was not yet ready, Ascari returned to Ferrari for the Italian Grand Prix. He fought Fangio for the lead at Monza before his engine failed.

1956.title: The title, with a teammate’s help.
1956.story: In the Lancia-Ferrari D50, Fangio won in Argentina, Britain and Germany; the Argentine win came in Luigi Musso’s car. Peter Collins handed over his car at Monaco and Monza, where second place sealed a fourth title.

1953.title: The race of the century.
1953.story: In his first Ferrari season, Hawthorn edged Fangio at Reims after a 60-lap duel for his first Grand Prix win. Two more podiums brought fourth place in the championship.

1954.title: Through fire to Pedralbes.
1954.story: Serious burns at the non-championship Syracuse race interrupted his year. Three second places, one shared with José Froilán González at the Nürburgring, preceded victory in the Spanish finale and third overall.

1955.title: A brief return.
1955.story: Hawthorn began the year with Vanwall and rejoined Ferrari mid-season. None of his three Ferrari starts reached the top five, and at Aintree he shared his car with Eugenio Castellotti.

1957.title: Second to Fangio’s charge.
1957.story: Back at Ferrari in the Lancia-Ferrari, Hawthorn did not win a championship race. His best result was second at the Nürburgring, where Fangio passed him on the penultimate lap.

1958.title: Britain’s first world champion.
1958.story: One win, at Reims, and five second places made Hawthorn champion by a single point from Stirling Moss. A season marked by the deaths of Luigi Musso and Peter Collins ended with his retirement.

1958.title: In service of a title.
1958.story: Hill’s first Ferrari Grand Prix came in a Formula Two Dino at the Nürburgring. Promoted to the works team, he finished third at Monza and in Morocco, where he let Hawthorn through to second.

1959.title: A first full season.
1959.story: Hill’s first full season with Ferrari brought second places at Reims and Monza and third at AVUS. Ferrari missed the British Grand Prix, and Hill finished fourth in the championship.

1960.title: The last front-engined winner.
1960.story: Ferrari’s front-engined Dino 246 was outpaced by rear-engined British cars. At a Monza boycotted by the main British teams, Hill led a Ferrari one-two-three: the last championship win for a front-engined car.

1961.title: Champion, at a cost.
1961.story: Wins at Spa and Monza made Hill the first American world champion. The title was settled at Monza, where teammate Wolfgang von Trips was killed in a crash that also killed spectators.

1962.title: A defence that faded.
1962.story: Hill began his title defence with three podiums, including second at Monaco, then scored no further points. It was his final season with Ferrari before he moved to ATS.

1963.title: From two wheels to red.
1963.story: The motorcycle world champion joined Ferrari and won the German Grand Prix, the team’s first victory in two years. Engine failures and a disqualification in Mexico limited the rest of his season.

1964.title: Champion on two and four wheels.
1964.story: Wins at the Nürburgring and Monza kept Surtees in contention. At the Mexican finale, in a NART-entered car painted white and blue, Bandini let him through to second and the title by one point.

1965.title: A season cut short.
1965.story: Without a win, Surtees took second in South Africa and third places in France and Britain. A serious sports car crash at Mosport in September ended his Formula One season early.

1966.title: Victory at Spa, then goodbye.
1966.story: In the new three-litre Ferrari, Surtees retired from the lead at Monaco and won a rain-hit Belgian Grand Prix from pole. A dispute with team manager Eugenio Dragoni at Le Mans led him to leave.

ascari.text: Ascari took his first championship victory from pole at the Nürburgring, as the Alfa Romeos struggled with overheating.
Pole, victory and fastest lap at Spa began a run in which Ascari won every remaining championship round of 1952.
Ascari won by a lap in the first championship race outside Europe, Indianapolis aside, a race marked by a crash that killed spectators.
After a long pit stop for carburettor trouble, Ascari rejoined third and passed Hawthorn and Farina to win at Bremgarten.

fangio.text: After his fuel pump failed, Fangio took over Luigi Musso’s car and won, receiving half points for the shared drive.
After damaging a wheel against a wall, Fangio took over Peter Collins’s car and finished second to Stirling Moss.
Fangio won from pole at the Nürburgring, ahead of Stirling Moss and Jean Behra.
With his own car out, Fangio took over Peter Collins’s Ferrari and finished second at Monza to clinch his fourth title.

hawthorn.text: Hawthorn beat Fangio after a 60-lap duel at Reims; the first four cars finished within five seconds of each other.
Hawthorn won the season finale at Pedralbes after several rivals, including Ascari in the new Lancia, retired.
Hawthorn led late on but finished second after Fangio repeatedly broke the lap record and passed him on the penultimate lap.
Second behind Moss at Casablanca, after Phil Hill let him through, made Hawthorn champion by one point.

phil_hill.text: Running second, Hill slowed on team orders to let Hawthorn through; Hill finished third and Hawthorn took the title.
Hill’s first Grand Prix win was the first by an American since 1921, excluding Indianapolis, and the last for a front-engined car.
Hill won from pole as Ferraris finished first to fourth at Spa, the last time any constructor achieved that result.
Hill won at Monza and clinched the title in a race where Wolfgang von Trips and spectators were killed.

surtees.text: Surtees passed Jim Clark’s misfiring Lotus to take his first championship win and Ferrari’s first for two years.
From pole, Surtees won at Monza as Clark and Graham Hill retired, bringing him into the championship fight.
Bandini let Surtees through to second on the final lap, giving him the title by one point from Graham Hill.
Surtees won from pole at Spa after a first-lap rainstorm eliminated several cars, in his last race for Ferrari.
